patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role: Sent abusers away and received them
patterns.role_note: Orán → Vatican: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta; Verona → Mendoza: Fr Nicola Corradi.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 1984: CONADEP, Nunca Más (1984) — children kidnapped and born in captivity.
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2025: Argentina — Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo: 140 stolen grandchildren identified
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: Dictatorship or occupation: children given to other families under false identities
patterns.role_note: Argentina — junta's 'systematic plan' to appropriate babies (2012 verdict). Argentina — Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo: 140 stolen grandchildren identified.
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Argentina — junta's 'systematic plan' to appropriate babies (2012 verdict); Argentina — Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo: 140 stolen grandchildren identified; Argentina — CONADEP 'Nunca Más': children of the disappeared taken and given to military families (1984); Marita Verón case — Tucumán brothel network.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 282 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Próvolo Institute, Luján de Cuyo (Mendoza) — convictions 2019
cases.who: Provolo Institute for the Deaf (Argentina branch); Fr Nicola Corradi, Fr Horacio Corbacho, gardener Armando Gómez; Sr Kumiko Kosaka charged
cases.what: Priests Nicola Corradi (Italian) and Horacio Corbacho and other staff of the Provolo school for deaf children in Luján de Cuyo, Mendoza were arrested in 2016, charged with abusing at least two dozen students. On 25 November 2019 a Mendoza court convicted Corradi, Corbacho and gardener Armando Gómez of abusing children at the school between 2004 and 2016; the victims in the trial were 10 former students. Corradi was sentenced to 42 years, Corbacho to 45 and Gómez to 18. Nun Kumiko Kosaka was charged in 2017 with helping the abuse and with physically abusing students.
cases.cover_up: Corradi had been accused in Verona in 2009 yet continued at the Argentine school; Japanese nun Kumiko Kosaka charged with abuse and covering up

cases.title: Argentina — junta's 'systematic plan' to appropriate babies (2012 verdict)
cases.who: Argentine military junta; armed forces and security forces; ESMA
cases.what: On 5 July 2012 Federal Oral Criminal Tribunal No. 6 of Buenos Aires found that the military junta had run a systematic plan to abduct children born to detained or disappeared mothers, between 1976 and 1983. Former dictator Jorge Videla was sentenced to 50 years and the last dictator, Reynaldo Bignone, to 15 years; nine other defendants received 15 to 40 years (MercoPress). The trial covered about 31–35 abductions. The tribunal convicted Bignone of crimes against humanity for implementing the plan.
cases.cover_up: Children's original identities were hidden and they were registered as the biological children of military families and regime allies.

cases.title: Wonderland Club / Operation Cathedral
cases.who: The Wonderland Club (encrypted online network)
cases.what: An international online ring that ran for about four years over encrypted internet chat; each new member had to supply 10,000 images of child abuse. Members held at least 750,000 images and 1,800 videos. Led by the UK National Crime Squad, police in 12 to 13 countries (reported figures differ) acted simultaneously on 2 September 1998, about 1,500 officers raiding 107 homes and making 104 arrests. CNN reported in February 2001 that only 17 of the children in the images had been identified, six of them in Britain. The investigation began after US Customs exposed a related ring, the Orchid Club, in 1996.

cases.title: Marita Verón case — Tucumán brothel network
cases.who: Brothel and trafficking ring in Tucumán province
cases.what: Marita Verón, aged 23, disappeared in Tucumán in 2002, allegedly abducted into forced prostitution. In December 2012 a Tucumán court acquitted all 13 defendants, provoking national protests and calls to impeach the judges. In December 2013 Tucumán's Supreme Court reversed the acquittals and found 10 of the 13 guilty. Her mother's foundation, created in 2008, says it has helped free hundreds of women and girls from brothels. (Verón was an adult; the case is included because it exposed the national network that also trafficked minors.)
cases.cover_up: Campaigners and the victim's family's lawyers said police were often paid to protect prostitution rings; trial court acquitted all 13 in 2012.

cases.title: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta of Orán — convicted 2022
cases.who: Diocese of Orán; Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta
cases.what: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta resigned from the Diocese of Orán in August 2017, citing health, after complaints from clergy, and in December 2017 Pope Francis gave him a post created for him at the Vatican's patrimony office (APSA). Clergy had complained to the nunciature in 2015–2016 about his behaviour with seminarians and explicit images on his phone. On 4 March 2022 a court in Salta sentenced him to four and a half years for continued sexual abuse of two former seminarians, aggravated by his being a minister of religion. Included as a case of a bishop moved to the Vatican, though the victims were adults.
cases.cover_up: After resigning in 2017 amid complaints he was given a post at the Vatican's APSA in December 2017; suspended in January 2019

cases.title: Uruguay — Gelman v. Uruguay: baby taken from disappeared mother (Operation Condor)
cases.who: Uruguayan Defense Information Service (SID); joint Argentine–Uruguayan commando under Operation Condor
cases.what: A pregnant 19-year-old Argentine detained in Buenos Aires in August 1976 was moved secretly to Montevideo, gave birth in a military hospital, and her baby was taken in December 1976 and left with a police officer's family, who raised her under another identity for 23 years. On 24 February 2011 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights found Uruguay responsible for enforced disappearance and suppression of the child's identity, and ruled the 1986 Expiry Law amnesty legally ineffective.
cases.cover_up: Uruguay's 1986 Expiry Law was used to close the investigation in 2003.

cases.title: Argentina — CONADEP 'Nunca Más': children of the disappeared taken and given to military families (1984)
cases.who: Argentine armed and security forces (1976–83)
cases.what: The National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons, created by President Raúl Alfonsín on 15 December 1983 and chaired by Ernesto Sábato, delivered its report Nunca Más on 20 September 1984. It recorded 8,960 forced disappearances between 1976 and 1983 and stated that no fewer than 200 children under 15 had been kidnapped; babies were taken with their parents or born to pregnant prisoners in detention camps and given to military families. The report was key evidence in the 1985 Trial of the Juntas.
cases.cover_up: Identities of children changed; records of births in detention not kept

cases.title: Argentina — Abuelas de Plaza de Mayo: 140 stolen grandchildren identified
cases.who: Argentine military regime (1976–83); military families and regime allies who received children
cases.what: The Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo were founded in 1977 to find children kidnapped with their disappeared parents or born to mothers in detention, who were passed for adoption to military families and regime allies. Their work led to the creation of Argentina's National Bank of Genetic Data. On 7 July 2025 they announced the 140th grandchild identified: a man born on 17 April 1977 at the clandestine centre 'La Escuelita' in Bahía Blanca after his parents were kidnapped in Cutral Có, Neuquén. The Grandmothers had found 97 grandchildren by 2008 and 133 by July 2023.
cases.cover_up: Children were illegally adopted with their original identities hidden; many did not know they were adopted.

cases.title: Argentina raids on The Family (Children of God) communes
cases.who: The Family / Children of God
cases.what: On 1 September 1993 Judge Roberto Marquevich ordered raids on Family communes near Buenos Aires; 137 children were taken into state custody and about 30 members arrested. The judge said nine children showed signs of 'cruel and atrocious maltreatment', which the group disputed. Children were later released after examination and no convictions resulted. Raids in Australia (1992, including Panton Hill, Victoria), France and Spain also ended without convictions.

cases.title: Paraguay — Fr Carlos Urrutigoity and the removal of Bishop Livieres
cases.who: Diocese of Ciudad del Este
cases.what: Argentine priest Carlos Urrutigoity was accused in 2002 in the US of sleeping with boarding-school students, giving them alcohol and sexually abusing a recently graduated seminarian. He then moved to the Diocese of Ciudad del Este, Paraguay, and became its second-in-command in 2014. His case reportedly cost Bishop Livieres his post when Pope Francis removed him in 2014. He was moved back to Mendoza, Argentina, in June 2015. He has not been convicted.
cases.cover_up: After accusations in the US (a 2002 complaint over students at St Gregory's Academy in the Diocese of Scranton), he moved with his group to Ciudad del Este, where Bishop Rogelio Livieres made him vicar general in 2014. Pope Francis removed Livieres in 2014; Urrutigoity left in June 2015. La Nación reported at least five Argentine priests accused of abuse or crimes against humanity had sheltered in Paraguay.

flows.title: Verona → Mendoza: Fr Nicola Corradi
flows.what: Corradi, accused at the Provolo deaf school in Verona in 2009 and flagged by the diocese in 2011, worked at the order's school in Argentina, where he was arrested in 2016 and in 2019 sentenced to 42 years for abusing deaf children.

flows.title: Orán → Vatican: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta
flows.what: After resigning amid clergy complaints in 2017, Zanchetta was given a post at the Vatican's patrimony office in December 2017; he was convicted in Argentina in 2022 of abusing two adult seminarians.

flows.title: Chile → Argentina (Schäfer in hiding 1997–2005)
flows.what: Charged with child abuse in Chile, Schäfer disappeared on 20 May 1997 and hid in Argentina until found in a gated community in Tortuguitas in March 2005 and returned to Chile.

networks.name: Argentine military junta — systematic appropriation of children (with Operation Condor partners)
networks.what: Federal Oral Tribunal No. 6 found in July 2012 that the junta ran a systematic plan to take children born to detained or disappeared mothers and give them to military families and regime allies; Videla received 50 years and Bignone 15. About 500 children are estimated to have been taken; 140 had been identified by July 2025.

networks.name: Colonia Dignidad / Villa Baviera
networks.what: German sect enclave in Chile led by Paul Schäfer, convicted in 2006 of abusing 25 minors. Used by Pinochet's secret police DINA as a detention and torture site (Rettig Commission 1991). Germany's president acknowledged diplomatic failures in 2016.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

networks.name: The Family International (Children of God)
networks.what: Founded by David Berg. A UK High Court judge found in 1995 that the group, including top leaders, had sexually abused minors in the past, and ordered it to denounce Berg's writings.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found South Asia lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cases.what: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.
cases.cover_up: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).

cases.title: Myanmar — Tatmadaw sexual violence against Rohingya and ethnic minority women, girls and boys (UN FFM)
cases.who: Myanmar armed forces (Tatmadaw)
cases.what: The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Myanmar found in 2018 that hundreds of Rohingya women and girls were raped during the 2017 'clearance operations', 80% of corroborated cases being gang rapes, and its August 2019 report found sexual and gender-based violence a 'hallmark' of Tatmadaw operations in Rakhine, Kachin and Shan. It documented Rohingya men and boys, some as young as twelve, detained at Buthidaung prison in 2012 and subjected to sexual violence.

cases.title: Norway — NOU 2026:7 finds illegal and unethical intercountry adoptions
cases.who: Norwegian adoption organisations; Norwegian authorities; partner orphanages and bodies in 12 countries
cases.what: A government committee appointed in 2023 presented NOU 2026:7 'Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit' on 22 June 2026. Examining adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s, it concluded there were illegal or unethical conditions and that the Norwegian adoption system had clear shortcomings throughout the period. Individual findings included a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother told she would get money if she consented, and documents deliberately falsified; payments to orphanages or organisations were sometimes linked to the number of children adopted.
cases.cover_up: Organisations did not always tell Norwegian authorities about payments or errors; authorities kept approving adoptions after learning of risks and illegalities.

cases.title: Kolkata red-light areas — rescues of trafficked Nepali girls and minors (2015, 2025)
cases.who: Brothel keepers and traffickers in Kolkata
cases.what: In January 2015 police, with International Justice Mission and three NGOs, freed six young women trafficked from Nepal from four brothels in Kolkata's largest red-light area; all had fake adult ID documents, which IJM said traffickers issue to underage girls. On 10 September 2025 Kolkata Police's Anti-Human Trafficking Unit rescued ten people including nine minor girls from a house in Burtolla, North Kolkata, and arrested six people, including the couple running it (charged). The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers recruit significant numbers of Nepali and Bangladeshi women and girls for sex trafficking in India.

cases.title: Bangladesh — girls trafficked to India, Pakistan and the Gulf; Rohingya girls near Cox's Bazar (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers, recruitment agents, armed groups in Rohingya camps
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit Bangladeshi women and girls in sex trafficking abroad, including in India, Pakistan and Gulf countries, and observers estimate children are 40 per cent of Bangladeshi sex-trafficking victims exploited abroad. Tourists have increased demand for sexual exploitation, including of Rohingya girls, near Cox's Bazar, where more than one million Rohingya refugees live in 33 camps. Courts convicted 103 traffickers, down from 407.
cases.cover_up: Corruption and official complicity were significant concerns; corrupt policing in Rohingya camps.

flows.what: Bangladeshi women and girls exploited in sex trafficking in India; children estimated at 40% of Bangladeshi sex-trafficking victims abroad.

cases.title: Swiss bar owner jailed 16 years for abusing more than 80 boys in Pattaya and northern Thailand
cases.who: Unnamed Swiss national (72, from Lucerne) who ran a bar in Pattaya
cases.what: A Swiss man previously convicted of abusing children in Fribourg (1980) and Valais (1991) returned to Thailand in 1996 and, mainly in 2002–2013, abused more than 80 boys in Pattaya, where he ran a bar with a hotel room frequented by Europeans, and in Nong Hoi in the north; he also forced boys to perform acts with European clients. Charged in Fribourg with human trafficking, encouraging prostitution, sexual acts with children and abuse material, he was sentenced by a Swiss court on 1 March 2018 to 16 years.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: Landslide Productions / Operations Avalanche and Ore
cases.who: Landslide Productions (payment portal, Thomas and Janice Reedy)
cases.what: Landslide, a Fort Worth, Texas portal run by Thomas and Janice Reedy, processed credit-card sign-ups for third-party sites, some offering child abuse images. US agents raided it in August 1999; a jury convicted Thomas Reedy, who was sentenced to 1,335 years (reduced to 180 on appeal), and Janice Reedy got 14 years. US Operation Avalanche examined about 35,000 names on the database, and the FBI passed details of 7,272 British residents to UK police, starting Operation Ore, Britain's biggest computer crime investigation; raids began in May 2002. CEOP said 140 children had been rescued in the UK. Later forensic examination showed large-scale credit card fraud in Landslide's records (54,348 sets of stolen card details), and some people were wrongly accused; a legal challenge in 2009 argued that many convictions for incitement rested on flawed credit-card evidence. Follow-on operations took place in other countries.
cases.cover_up: Later reconstruction of the Landslide data found many listed names were victims of credit-card fraud, and the validity of UK Operation Ore procedures was questioned; an estimated 33 suicides followed in the UK.

cases.title: University of Zurich pilot study — Catholic Church in Switzerland
cases.who: Swiss Bishops' Conference and religious orders (commissioned study)
cases.what: Historians at the University of Zurich, led by Monika Dommann and Marietta Meier and commissioned by the Swiss Bishops' Conference and religious orders, published a pilot study in September 2023 on sexual abuse in the Swiss Catholic Church since the mid-20th century. They documented 1,002 cases involving 510 accused people and 921 victims; 74% of the documents concerned abuse of minors. More than half the cases occurred in pastoral work and about 30% in Catholic children's homes, schools and boarding schools. The researchers called the cases 'the tip of the iceberg' and found that church criminal law was hardly ever applied, with many cases kept secret, covered up or trivialised.

cases.title: Territorial Abbey of Saint-Maurice — independent working group report (2025)
cases.who: Abbey of Saint-Maurice (canons regular) and its boarding school, Valais
cases.what: An independent working group formed at the request of the abbey, then under a Vatican-appointed apostolic administrator, by Neuchâtel attorney general Pierre Aubert presented its findings on 20 June 2025. Historians of the University of Fribourg (Anne-Françoise Praz, Stéphanie Roulin and others) and retired judge Claire-Lise Mayor Aubert heard about 50 witnesses and 24 clergy and examined sexual violence at the abbey and its boarding school from 1960 to 2024. They found sexualised touching by canons, ambiguous photo sessions, exhibitionism and use of child abuse material; since 1970 five criminal penalty orders had been issued against three canons and a novice, and members with ambiguous or unlawful conduct were left in office without precautions. The mandate did not cover the abbey's collège.

cases.title: Swiss administrative detention and forced placements (incl. Verdingkinder)
cases.who: Swiss cantonal and municipal authorities; about 650 institutions
cases.what: The Independent Expert Commission on Administrative Detention, set up under the Federal Act of 21 March 2014, presented its final report on 2 September 2019. It found more than 60,000 people were interned in about 650 institutions without court order, mainly from 1930 to 1981, and that victims were abused physically, psychologically and sexually. The Swiss government had apologised in 2010; a 2016 law created a CHF 25,000 'solidarity contribution' for victims of compulsory measures, including children placed as indentured farm labourers (Verdingkinder).

cases.title: Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption
cases.who: Baby farms, brokers, hospital doctors and nurses acting as intermediaries for Western agencies
cases.what: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. Sri Lanka changed its rules after a 1987 police raid found 20 newborns and 22 women held in 'prison like conditions'.
cases.cover_up: Adoption records were widely falsified; 'acting mothers' were paid to pose as birth mothers in court.

cases.title: Switzerland — authorities' irregularities in intercountry adoptions (Sri Lanka, India, Tibet…); proposed ban
cases.who: Swiss federal and cantonal authorities; private adoption agencies
cases.what: Swiss authorities soon realised that the placement of children for adoption, often wrongly presented as orphans, was also driven by economic interests and linked to organised child trafficking; decisions were often made on incomplete or falsified documents, and checks on foster families and on legal requirements were insufficient. From the 2010s, under pressure from groups such as Back to the Roots, intercountry adoptions from Tibet, Sri Lanka and India drew public attention. In 2018 the Federal Assembly commissioned a study on intercountry adoption; the Federal Council acknowledged the authorities' irregularities and omissions in 2020 and 2023, and at the end of 2024 recommended a general ban on intercountry adoption.

cases.who: The Com (decentralised online network incl. 764, CVLT)
cases.what: Coordinated by Europol's European Counter Terrorism Centre with EU states, Norway, Switzerland, the UK, US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand (28 countries). cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. cases.title: Norway-led crypto-tracing operation: 28 arrests (2026)
cases.who: Buyers paying cryptocurrency for dark web forum access
cases.what: From late May to mid-June 2026 police in Canada, Czechia, Germany, Norway, Poland, Sweden and Switzerland arrested 28 men aged 22–54 suspected of paying cryptocurrency to access dark web forums with abuse videos; one used AI to generate material and some victims were family members. Norwegian police used a crypto-tracing method developed in 2025, which also identified two sellers.

cases.title: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
cases.who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
cases.what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

All four were implicated in the petitions (Guardian, 2023).

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2022: Truth Commission (CEV) final report volume 'No es un mal menor' on children in the armed conflict (2022).
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 20,864 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman).
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: War and the taking of children
patterns.role: Abductions and sexual violence by armed groups
patterns.role_note: Colombia — FARC-EP recruitment and use of children (JEP Macro-case 07). Colombia — sexual violence against girls by ELN, FARC dissidents, Clan del Golfo (UN verified).
patterns.pattern_summary: Armed groups have abducted, enslaved and sold children as a deliberate practice. In 2014 the group calling itself Islamic State captured Yazidi women and children in northern Iraq and sold girls as sexual slaves; a UN commission reported in 2016 that more than 3,200 women and children were still held. In 2014 Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok in north-eastern Nigeria, and 82 were still captive in 2024. The Lord's Resistance Army abducted children in Uganda and the neighbouring countries over many years; in 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted one of its commanders, Dominic Ongwen, on 61 counts, including forced marriage and sexual slavery. UN fact-finding missions found sexual violence against children by Myanmar's army and by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, against girls as young as eight. The UN verifies and publishes these attacks country by country each year.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Colombia — sexual violence against girls by ELN, FARC dissidents, Clan del Golfo (UN verified); Colombia — Truth Commission volume on children: 16,238 recruited; recruited girls subjected to rape, forced contraception and abortion (2022); Cartagena — 'La Madame' network exploiting girls for tourists (plea 2018); Colombia — Tren de Aragua sex trafficking of Venezuelan girls; webcam industry (US TIP 2025).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 282 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No national inquiry into institutional abuse found
patterns.role_note: Archdiocese ordered to disclose files on 915 accused clergy cases to journalist Juan Pablo Barrientos within 48 hours; full compliance not achieved
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Medellín — US federal prosecutions of travelling offenders (10 convictions by May 2026)
cases.who: US-national travelling offenders; HSI Colombia; Alcaldía de Medellín
cases.what: BluRadio reported on 21 May 2026 that US courts, working with Colombian authorities and the Medellín mayor's office, had handed down a tenth sentence in an offensive against foreigners exploiting children in Medellín: Ramón Arellano Sandoval, 65, sentenced in Miami to 30 years for attempted sexual exploitation of a 14-year-old Medellín girl, who had entered the city 48 times in two years. On 22 January 2026 Manuel Poceiro, 69, of Miami, was sentenced to life for travelling to Colombia to exploit minors, after HSI found material involving at least five minors. cases.title: Cartagena — 'La Madame' network exploiting girls for tourists (plea 2018)
cases.who: Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello ('La Madame')
cases.what: Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello ran a sex network from a Bocagrande apartment in Cartagena, supplying young women and minors to parties on yachts, in hotels and at beaches and sending women to Panama, Mexico, Miami and the Bahamas; prosecutors seized 15 ledgers of clients and payments, and a WhatsApp group listed 200 women. In 2018 she accepted charges of human trafficking and conspiracy in a plea deal and was sentenced to eight years and one month; she was released on parole in 2023. US ICE supported the investigation.
cases.cover_up: At hearings she threatened to reveal the names of politicians and powerful men she said were clients (her claim, unverified).

cases.title: Colombia — Truth Commission volume on children: 16,238 recruited; recruited girls subjected to rape, forced contraception and abortion (2022)
cases.who: FARC-EP, ELN and other guerrillas, paramilitary groups, and state security forces (recruitment and use of minors)
cases.what: Colombia's Commission for the Clarification of Truth published its volume on children and adolescents, 'No es un mal menor', in July 2022. It documented 16,238 children recruited by armed groups between 1990 and 2017 and estimated the real number at 27,101 to 40,828, and described recruitment as intentional and systematic, including use of minors by the state security forces. It found that recruited girls were forced to use contraception at an early age, forced to have abortions, and subjected to harassment, rape and sexual torture.

cases.title: Colombia — sexual violence against girls by ELN, FARC dissidents, Clan del Golfo (UN verified)
cases.who: ELN, FARC-EP dissident groups, Clan del Golfo; Colombian armed forces (2 cases 2023)
cases.what: The UN verified sexual violence against 33 girls in Colombia in 2024, by the ELN (12), FARC-EP dissident groups (12), Clan del Golfo (7) and unidentified perpetrators. In 2023 it verified 26 cases, including 2 by the Colombian armed forces.

cases.title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cases.what: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.
cases.cover_up: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).

cases.title: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
cases.who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations
cases.what: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.

cases.title: Norway — NOU 2026:7 finds illegal and unethical intercountry adoptions
cases.who: Norwegian adoption organisations; Norwegian authorities; partner orphanages and bodies in 12 countries
cases.what: A government committee appointed in 2023 presented NOU 2026:7 'Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit' on 22 June 2026. Examining adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s, it concluded there were illegal or unethical conditions and that the Norwegian adoption system had clear shortcomings throughout the period. Individual findings included a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother told she would get money if she consented, and documents deliberately falsified; payments to orphanages or organisations were sometimes linked to the number of children adopted.
cases.cover_up: Organisations did not always tell Norwegian authorities about payments or errors; authorities kept approving adoptions after learning of risks and illegalities.

Former secretariat members have publicly acknowledged responsibility.

cases.who: Instituto Colombiano de Bienestar Familiar (ICBF) substitute-home (hogar sustituto) programme
cases.what: In March 2018 the ICBF opened 21 investigations into foster homes nationwide for alleged verbal abuse, poor food and neglect and relocated 44 children and 14 adolescents, with about 3,100 homes still to review. cases.who: Adoption trafficking ring
cases.what: In 1981 the New York Times (Warren Hoge) reported that Colombian authorities had uncovered a multimillion-dollar ring in which hundreds of poor Andean children were taken or bought from their mothers and sold abroad with forged papers. cases.title: Colombia — Tren de Aragua sex trafficking of Venezuelan girls; webcam industry (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Tren de Aragua; ELN; webcam studios
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says Tren de Aragua and the ELN run sex-trafficking networks in Villa del Rosario, Norte de Santander, and Tren de Aragua uses Cúcuta's transport hub to move victims to Argentina, Ecuador and Peru and operates in Bogotá, Cali, Medellín and Pereira. Traffickers recruit women and girls, mostly Colombians and displaced Venezuelans, into 'webcam modelling', an industry likely worth over $1.2 billion a year. Sex trafficking of girls is prevalent in tourist areas and extractive zones.
cases.cover_up: Two complicit officials received plea-deal sentences of 7.5 years, below the statutory minimum.

cases.title: Colombia — Constitutional Court orders Medellín archdiocese to release priests' files
cases.who: Archdiocese of Medellín; Salesian Inspectorate of San Luis Beltrán, Medellín
cases.what: In May 2019 journalist Juan Pablo Barrientos, author of 'Dejad que los niños vengan a mí', asked the Archdiocese of Medellín and the Salesians for the records of 43 priests, including complaints against them. After both refused, he filed tutela actions. On 3 March 2020 the Constitutional Court ruled that the information was semi-private and that the right to information prevailed, ordering the archdiocese to hand it over. In 2022 the Court agreed to review a further petition covering 915 priests who served in Medellín.
cases.cover_up: Both the archdiocese and the Salesian province refused journalist Juan Pablo Barrientos's 2019 request for the records of 43 priests, calling them private; the archdiocese appealed the first-instance ruling against it.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: Dictatorship or occupation: children given to other families under false identities
patterns.role_note: Spain — children of Republican prisoners taken by the Franco regime. Spain — Dr Eduardo Vela, first 'stolen baby' trial: guilty but not punished.
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Morocco — royal pardon of Spanish child rapist Daniel Galván (2013)
cases.who: Daniel Galván Viña
cases.what: Daniel Galván Viña, a retired Spanish professor, was arrested in Morocco in December 2010 and in September 2011 sentenced to 30 years for raping 11 Moroccan children aged 4 to 14. In late July 2013 he was among 48 Spanish prisoners pardoned by King Mohammed VI; after protests outside parliament in Rabat, the king revoked the pardon on 4 August 2013, citing the gravity of the crimes and the victims' rights, and said he had not been told the details of the case. Galván had already left Morocco; he was later arrested in Spain.
cases.cover_up: King Mohammed VI pardoned Galván on 30 July 2013 among 48 Spanish prisoners; he left Morocco on an expired passport with authorities' knowledge before the pardon was cancelled. Protesters in Rabat were violently dispersed. A 2010 US cable reported a 2006 royal pardon of a French man convicted of abusing a 15-year-old boy in Marrakesh.

cases.title: Welcome to Video — darknet CSAM site run from South Korea
cases.who: Welcome to Video (operator Son Jong-woo / Son Jung-woo)
cases.what: A Korean-run darknet site that sold access to child sexual abuse videos for Bitcoin; it held over 250,000 unique videos and its server had more than one million Bitcoin addresses, one per account. IRS-CI tracing of Bitcoin transactions located the server in South Korea, and the operator, Son Jong-woo, was arrested on 5 March 2018. On 16 October 2019 the US DOJ announced 337 users arrested and charged, with leads sent to 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 arrests in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). He served 18 months in South Korea; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused US extradition, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. DOJ said 45% of the videos analysed had not been known before.
cases.cover_up: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.

cases.title: Regpay — Minsk-based paid abuse sites / Operation Falcon
cases.who: Regpay Co. Ltd (Belarus) with Florida payment firm Connections
cases.what: Regpay Co. Ltd of Minsk, Belarus, processed paid memberships to about 50 websites, including child abuse sites it operated itself, serving thousands of subscribers worldwide; payments were laundered with help from Connections USA of Fort Lauderdale, Florida. US Attorney General John Ashcroft announced the case in January 2004 as part of Operation Falcon. Regpay's president Yahor Zalatarou and marketing director Alexei Buchnev were arrested at a Paris hotel on 30 July 2003 after a ruse by US agents, and technical administrator Aliaksandr Boika was arrested in Tarragona, Spain, on 31 July 2003 and extradited. All pleaded guilty in New Jersey. Buchnev was sentenced to 40 months in May 2006; Zalatarou and Boika were each sentenced to 25 years on 9 August 2006. Connections' chief executive pleaded guilty to money laundering. Hundreds of subscribers were arrested in the US and other countries.

cases.title: Spain — children of Republican prisoners taken by the Franco regime
cases.who: Franco regime; Auxilio Social; Women's Protection Board (Patronato de Protección a la Mujer); Falange
cases.what: A 1940 law allowed imprisoned mothers to keep children only until age three, after which the state took custody; 12,043 Republican children were in state custody in 1943. In 2008 Judge Baltasar Garzón characterised the removals as crimes against humanity and said the Falange was involved in kidnapping or forcibly repatriating children and changing their names. In January 2011 families of 261 babies who disappeared from hospitals over about fifty years took their cases to the attorney general; lawyers' estimates of up to 300,000 were rejected by a 2026 forensic study, which did not dispute about 30,000 children placed in state care.
cases.cover_up: Names were changed so children could be given to pro-regime families; the 1977 Amnesty Law has hindered investigation, and many Women's Protection Board files went missing in 1996.

cases.title: El Salvador — children disappeared by the armed forces during the civil war (Pro-Búsqueda)
cases.who: Salvadoran armed forces
cases.what: Pro-Búsqueda, founded in 1994, has documented close to a thousand children disappeared during the Salvadoran civil war, mostly by the armed forces; many were adopted through flawed procedures to the US, France, Spain, Italy and the Netherlands. On 1 March 2005 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled on the 1982 disappearance of the Serrano Cruz sisters during the 'Guinda de Mayo' military operation. El Salvador created a National Search Commission for Disappeared Children in 2010.
cases.cover_up: The armed forces have not granted access to archives on disappeared children despite years of lobbying.

cases.title: Catalonia — Síndic de Greuges (ombudsman) report on child sexual abuse in the Catholic Church (2020)
cases.who: Catholic religious congregations and dioceses in Catalonia
cases.what: A commission within the Catalan ombudsman's office (Síndic de Greuges), under Rafael Ribó, published its report on 2 October 2020. Most cases it heard concerned boys aged 5 to 17, abused repeatedly in the 1960s and 1970s on camps and excursions, on church premises and in abusers' flats, with three cases from the 1990s; documents pointed to many more victims than came forward. Religious congregations generally had not looked for other cases or offered reparation. Among seven recommendations, it asked the Catalan Parliament to create an inquiry commission, which the Parliament approved on 27 April 2022.
cases.cover_up: Congregations generally did not seek out other cases or offer reparation.

cases.title: Mallorca — Consell de Mallorca commission on sexual exploitation of children in IMAS care (2021)
cases.who: Institut Mallorquí d'Afers Socials (IMAS), the island's child-protection agency
cases.what: A commission of the Consell de Mallorca, chaired by vice-president Jaume Tortella, reported on 23 April 2021 on the sexual exploitation of minors in the care of the island's child-protection agency IMAS; about 16 cases were known in January 2020, 13 of them from 2017 to early 2019. With the PP and Vox refusing to take part, it found no political, technical or criminal responsibility and no network linking the cases, matching the prosecutors' investigation. Reporting had changed in February 2020 so that suspicions go to the national police, and five cases not previously reported were sent to prosecutors. In late 2020 two men were convicted of corrupting girls in care, and in April 2022 a European Parliament Petitions Committee delegation visited Palma to examine the cases.

cases.title: Spanish Ombudsman report on Church abuse
cases.who: Catholic Church in Spain
cases.what: Spain's first official inquiry into clergy abuse, a nearly 800-page report by Ombudsman Ángel Gabilondo presented to parliament on 27 October 2023 after an 18-month investigation of 487 cases, criticised the church's response as often minimising or denying the problem. A GAD3 survey of 8,000 adults in the report found 1.13% said they had been abused as children by clergy or lay church members and 0.6% by clergy. Gabilondo did not extrapolate a victim count; media applying the percentages to Spain's adult population put the figure at about 440,000 (or about 200,000 for clergy alone). The Spanish bishops apologised but disputed the media figures.

cases.title: Spain — Cremades & Calvo-Sotelo audit for the Episcopal Conference (2023)
cases.who: Spanish Episcopal Conference; Catholic clergy, religious and lay church staff
cases.what: The Spanish Episcopal Conference hired the law firm Cremades & Calvo-Sotelo in February 2022 to audit sexual abuse in the Church. The church announced its findings on 21 December 2023: at least 2,056 minor victims and 1,383 complaints, without saying how many clergy were accused. The figure is far below the estimate of more than 200,000 victims since 1940 published in October 2023 by an independent commission appointed by parliament, and the bishops said it was 'obvious that the number is higher'.

cases.title: Marcial Maciel and the Legion of Christ — 2019 internal report
cases.who: Legion of Christ (Legionaries); founder Marcial Maciel
cases.what: For decades until 2006 the Vatican dismissed accusations by seminarians that founder Marcial Maciel had abused them. In 2006 it ordered him to retire to a life of 'prayer and penitence', and on 1 May 2010, after an apostolic visitation, it said his acts were 'true crimes'. The Legion's own report, released on 21 December 2019, found that 175 minors were abused by 33 of its priests between 1941 and 2019; at least 60 of them by Maciel. It said 111 of the 175 were victims of Maciel or of his victims, and that 14 of the 33 abusive priests had themselves been abused within the order.
cases.cover_up: Letters to the Vatican in 1976, 1978 and 1989 and formal charges in 1998 produced no action; Vatican in 2010 said the Legion had shielded Maciel; Maciel never laicised or tried

cases.title: Society of Jesus in Spain — report on abuse since 1927 (2021)
cases.who: Society of Jesus (Jesuits), Spain — 65 of the 96 accused abused children
cases.what: In January 2021 the Jesuits in Spain published a report admitting 118 cases of sexual abuse since 1927, 81 of them against children and 37 against adults. It named 96 accused Jesuits, about 1.08% of members since 1927; of the 65 who abused children, 48 had died and 17 were alive. AP described it as the first comprehensive internal inquiry into abuse by a religious order in Spain. Victims' groups criticised it for not naming perpetrators or those who covered up abuse.

cases.title: Marist Brothers in Spain — independent commission recognises 25 victims (2020)
cases.who: Marist Brothers (Hermanos Maristas) schools in Spain, incl. Barcelona
cases.what: On 3 December 2020 the Marist congregation in Spain announced that an independent commission it had set up to review all cases had recognised 25 victims of sexual abuse by former teachers in its schools, with compensation reported at about 400,000 euros in total, including for time-barred cases. The Barcelona cases, from 1970 to 2010, were exposed by local press in 2016. Only one teacher, lay PE teacher Joaquín Benítez, was tried; in 2019 he was sentenced to 21 years and nine months for abusing four pupils, other complaints being time-barred.

cases.title: Romania — post-1989 adoption trade and 2004 ban
cases.who: Private adoption agencies and intermediaries; Romanian authorities
cases.what: After Ceaușescu's fall, television images of about 100,000 children in orphanages led to an adoption boom; private agencies charged €7,500–25,000 and the system 'quickly became awash in corruption' (DW). Romania halted adoptions in June 1991 and, under EU pressure, passed a law in June 2004 banning all foreign adoptions except by grandparents. The European Parliament's rapporteur Baroness Emma Nicholson had criticised 'international adoption and child trafficking' in Romania. Romania's own HCCH return shows 458 intercountry adoptions in 2002, 332 in 2003, 2 in 2005 and 0 in 2006.

cases.title: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)
cases.who: Orphanages and foreign adoption agencies operating in Ethiopia
cases.what: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

cases.title: China — intercountry adoption programme ended (2024) after trafficking cases
cases.who: China Center for Children's Welfare and Adoption; state orphanages
cases.what: China opened intercountry adoption in 1992; about 160,000 children were sent abroad, peaking at almost 8,000 to the US in 2005. The programme came to depend increasingly on abuse, abduction and trafficking (New Yorker), including Hunan orphanages buying trafficked babies (2005). On 5 September 2024 the foreign ministry announced the end of the programme, except adoption by blood relatives or of a stepchild.

flows.title: Bucharest → Spain
flows.what: Romanian intercountry adoptions to Spain in 2002, during the moratorium period before the 2004 ban.

flows.title: Europe → Tangier, Morocco (tourist offenders in vacation rentals)
flows.what: NGOs report tourists exploit children in Tangier in vacation rentals owned and managed by European nationals.

networks.name: Franco regime child removals and Spain's 'stolen babies'
networks.what: The Franco regime, Auxilio Social and the Women's Protection Board removed about 30,000 children of Republican prisoners and took babies of confined women into the early 1980s; later hospital 'stolen baby' cases reached the courts from 2011, with the first trial (Dr Eduardo Vela, 2018) ending in acquittal on limitation grounds.

networks.name: Welcome to Video
networks.what: Darknet video site paid in Bitcoin, about 1.2 million members; seized 2018. 337 arrests in 38 countries announced October 2019. Start year 2015 is not in the sources opened and is omitted from cases.

networks.name: Boylover forum
networks.what: 'Discussion-only' forum used to make contact before sharing abuse material privately; 670 suspects, 184 arrests, 230 children safeguarded (Operation Rescue, 2011).

networks.name: Kidflix
networks.what: Paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users (2022–2025), 91,000 videos; 1,393 suspects identified, 79 arrested.

networks.name: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
networks.what: Not one organisation: thousands of local traffickers, often parents or relatives, paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse. IJM: 1 in 100 Filipino children affected in 2022.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

networks.name: Legion of Christ (Legionaries of Christ)
networks.what: Founded in Mexico in 1941 by Marcial Maciel. The Vatican said in 2010 that Maciel committed 'true crimes' and the Legion had shielded him, and placed it under a papal delegate. The Legion's December 2019 report acknowledged 175 minors abused 1941–2019, 60 by Maciel and the rest by 33 priests.

networks.name: Marist Brothers
networks.what: Teaching order founded in France. Listed 154 members accused in Australia (1980–2015); nine Brothers convicted in New Zealand; apologised for systemic abuse at Scottish schools; acknowledged at least 14 victims of one Brother in Chile; complaints against 12 teachers at Barcelona schools.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role_note: 2003: The Gambia: Tourism Offences Act 2003 (child = under 18; hotel operators liable for knowingly allowing child prostitution) 2017: US TIP: traffickers in The Gambia increasingly host child sex tourists in private residences outside the commercial tourist areas, making detection harder
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found West and Central Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Belgium (Flanders) — expert panel and Ethiopia investigation on intercountry adoption malpractice
cases.who: Flemish adoption services; intermediaries in Ethiopia and other countries of origin
cases.what: After reports of malpractice in adoptions from Ethiopia in 2019, the Flemish government appointed an independent expert panel on intercountry adoption, which delivered its findings in 2021 (final report dated 15 February 2023), and funded the Flemish Centre for Adoption to examine Ethiopian adoptions from 1997 to 2015. Preliminary conclusions found that the true story sometimes differed from the adoption files and that in the worst cases children had not been given up voluntarily by their birth parents. The panel's report led to screening of every country of origin, after which Flanders stopped adoptions from Vietnam and then from Gambia, Haiti and Morocco.

cases.title: The Gambia — child sex tourism on the Senegambia Strip (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Organized networks using European and Gambian travel agencies
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says European tourists, primarily from the UK, reportedly travel to The Gambia to exploit children, and that organized sex-trafficking networks use European and Gambian travel agencies to promote the country as a destination, especially the Senegambia Strip. Women and girls from other West African countries, especially Nigeria, are recruited for tourism jobs and then sexually exploited. The Tourism Offences Act provides life imprisonment for child trafficking by tourists.

flows.title: United Kingdom → The Gambia (travelling offenders)
flows.what: European tourists, primarily from the UK, reportedly travel to The Gambia to exploit children; networks use European and Gambian travel agencies.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2018: Isle of Man — Tynwald committee report on Knottfield children's home.
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Isle of Man — Knottfield children's home (Tynwald committee report).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 282 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Isle of Man — Knottfield children's home (Tynwald committee report)
cases.who: Knottfield children's home (Isle of Man Government); house parent Joseph Marshall
cases.what: A Tynwald scrutiny committee (Social Affairs Policy Review Committee) chaired by David Cretney reported on 6 October 2018 on the 'horrific physical, emotional and sexual abuse' by Joseph Marshall while he ran Knottfield children's home with his wife between 1973 and 1983, and made 11 recommendations. Marshall had been convicted of 13 offences relating to Knottfield in 1992 and was jailed for six years in April 2022 for sexually abusing two boys there. The report was withdrawn during the criminal case; the Isle of Man Government apologised on 16 January 2023 for mistakes that contributed to the abuse and supported all 11 recommendations.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role: Sent abusers away and received them
patterns.role_note: Verona → Mendoza: Fr Nicola Corradi; Phoenix → Rome: Joseph Henn (fugitive 2003–2019).
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Lateran concordat and Italian reporting (2012): —
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 2 documented adoption flows into Italy on this map.
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: Dictatorship or occupation: children given to other families under false identities
patterns.role_note: El Salvador — children disappeared by the armed forces during the civil war (Pro-Búsqueda) (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.
