cases.title: Próvolo Institute, Luján de Cuyo (Mendoza) — convictions 2019
cases.who: Provolo Institute for the Deaf (Argentina branch); Fr Nicola Corradi, Fr Horacio Corbacho, gardener Armando Gómez; Sr Kumiko Kosaka charged
cases.what: Priests Nicola Corradi (Italian) and Horacio Corbacho and other staff of the Provolo school for deaf children in Luján de Cuyo, Mendoza were arrested in 2016, charged with abusing at least two dozen students. On 25 November 2019 a Mendoza court convicted Corradi, Corbacho and gardener Armando Gómez of abusing children at the school between 2004 and 2016; the victims in the trial were 10 former students. Corradi was sentenced to 42 years, Corbacho to 45 and Gómez to 18. Nun Kumiko Kosaka was charged in 2017 with helping the abuse and with physically abusing students.
cases.cover_up: Corradi had been accused in Verona in 2009 yet continued at the Argentine school; Japanese nun Kumiko Kosaka charged with abuse and covering up

cases.title: Italy — Il Forteto community, Tuscany: abuse of children placed by courts
cases.who: Il Forteto agricultural cooperative and community; Tuscany Region, juvenile court and local authorities that placed and accredited it
cases.what: Il Forteto, a cooperative and community at Vicchio in the Mugello near Florence, received children placed by juvenile courts and social services for decades. Its founder, Rodolfo Fiesoli, was definitively sentenced to 14 years and 10 months for abuse, although a conviction had already become final in 1985 and placements continued. Two Tuscan regional council inquiry commissions examined the case; a parliamentary inquiry in the previous legislature did not finish with a final report, and a new bicameral commission of inquiry was created by Law 47 of 25 March 2024 and installed on 1 August 2024. Its task is to establish institutional responsibilities and why authorities kept accrediting the community after court rulings on abuse and mistreatment.
cases.cover_up: The founder already had a final conviction in 1985, yet courts and social services kept placing children there; parliament's 2024 commission is to establish why authorities kept accrediting the community after court rulings on sexual abuse and mistreatment.

cases.title: Hugh Nelson — first UK prosecution for AI-made abuse images
cases.who: Individual offender selling commissioned AI-transformed images
cases.what: Nelson, 27, used 3D software with an AI function to turn ordinary photos of real children, some supplied by people who knew them, into abuse imagery, selling it in chatrooms for about £5,000 over 18 months. Greater Manchester Police caught him after he told an undercover officer he charged £80 per 'character'. Convicted of 16 offences including encouraging the rape of a child under 13, he was sentenced at Bolton Crown Court on 28 October 2024 to 18 years. Police identified suspects and victims in Italy, France and the US.

cases.title: Wonderland Club / Operation Cathedral
cases.who: The Wonderland Club (encrypted online network)
cases.what: An international online ring that ran for about four years over encrypted internet chat; each new member had to supply 10,000 images of child abuse. Members held at least 750,000 images and 1,800 videos. Led by the UK National Crime Squad, police in 12 to 13 countries (reported figures differ) acted simultaneously on 2 September 1998, about 1,500 officers raiding 107 homes and making 104 arrests. CNN reported in February 2001 that only 17 of the children in the images had been identified, six of them in Britain. The investigation began after US Customs exposed a related ring, the Orchid Club, in 1996.

cases.title: Black Axe in Palermo — 14 convicted (2018), 4 acquitted of mafia association (2019)
cases.who: Black Axe (Nigerian confraternity) cell in Palermo
cases.what: A Palermo police operation on 18 November 2016 arrested 19 alleged members of a Black Axe cell based in the Ballarò district; prosecutors said it ran debt collection, exploitation of prostitution and drug trafficking with mafia-style initiation rites. On 21 May 2018 a Palermo judge (fast-track procedure) convicted 14 Nigerians to a combined 87 years. In November 2019 the Palermo Corte d'Assise, trying five others, did not accept the mafia-association charge: four were acquitted and one was jailed for 11 years for kidnapping and sexual violence.

cases.title: El Salvador — children disappeared by the armed forces during the civil war (Pro-Búsqueda)
cases.who: Salvadoran armed forces
cases.what: Pro-Búsqueda, founded in 1994, has documented close to a thousand children disappeared during the Salvadoran civil war, mostly by the armed forces; many were adopted through flawed procedures to the US, France, Spain, Italy and the Netherlands. On 1 March 2005 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled on the 1982 disappearance of the Serrano Cruz sisters during the 'Guinda de Mayo' military operation. El Salvador created a National Search Commission for Disappeared Children in 2010.
cases.cover_up: The armed forces have not granted access to archives on disappeared children despite years of lobbying.

cases.title: Guatemala — Peace Archives report: army and state role in adoptions of children during the war (1977–1989)
cases.who: Guatemalan armed forces and National Police; Secretaría de Bienestar Social (Hogar Elisa Martínez); notaries and courts
cases.what: In September 2009 the Dirección de los Archivos de la Paz, part of the Peace Secretariat of the Presidency set up under President Álvaro Colom, published a study of adoptions during the internal armed conflict. It reviewed 333 of 670 adoption files recorded for 1977–1989 and found that the army and National Police transported children into the adoption system, that adoptions often rested on court declarations of abandonment with little effort to find parents, and that a 1977 decree let notaries formalise adoptions without a judge. Chief investigator Marco Tulio Álvarez told the press the children went mainly to the United States, Sweden, Italy and France.
cases.cover_up: Decree 54-77 (1977) let notaries complete adoptions without prior judicial approval; the welfare secretariat kept no record of how many children it received

cases.title: Diocese of Bolzano-Bressanone — Westpfahl Spilker Wastl report (2025)
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Bolzano-Bressanone (South Tyrol)
cases.what: The Munich law firm Westpfahl Spilker Wastl, commissioned by the Diocese of Bolzano-Bressanone, published its 631-page report on 20 January 2025, described as the first fully independent study of its kind in Italy, covering 1964 to 2023. It found 29 clerics against whom allegations were proven or highly probable, in 67 cases of sexual assault with 59 victims, plus 16 unclear cases; one priest abused girls as young as seven and was removed only in 2010. It described the handling of cases until 2010 as a general and highly systemic failure. Bishop Ivo Muser said 'every case is one too many' and that victims' suffering should fill the church with shame.
cases.cover_up: Handling of abuse cases until 2010 was a systemic failure; one priest was removed only in 2010 despite allegations from the 1960s.

cases.title: Chile — Chamber of Deputies commission on irregular adoptions (2019)
cases.who: Hospital medical and paramedical staff, Civil Registry staff, private intermediary organisations
cases.what: A special investigating commission of the Chamber of Deputies, chaired by Deputy Boris Barrera, worked from January to 22 July 2019 on children taken from mainly poor, often rural mothers, some of whom were made to believe their babies had died, and given for adoption, many abroad, before, during and after the 1973–1990 dictatorship. It found complicity by medical and paramedical staff, Civil Registry staff and organisations operating outside hospitals, and noted that private intermediaries were paid for their role. It recommended an international DNA bank, a national truth commission on irregular adoptions and excluding private bodies from adoption; the Chamber approved the report on 4 October 2019 by 88 votes with 13 abstentions.
cases.cover_up: Some hospitals did not register or destroyed birth records from 1970 onward (e.g. Carlos Van Buren hospital, Valparaíso); the commission also found gaps in birth and departure records

cases.title: Europol: at least 10,000 unaccompanied migrant children missing in Europe (2016)
cases.who: Europol; organized crime exploiting the migrant flow
cases.what: On 31 January 2016 Europol's chief of staff Brian Donald told The Observer that at least 10,000 unaccompanied children had disappeared after arriving in Europe, 5,000 of them in Italy and 1,000 in Sweden, and that Europol had evidence some had been sexually exploited. He said an entire criminal infrastructure had developed over 18 months around exploiting the migrant flow, with many arrests in Germany and Hungary. Save the Children estimated 26,000 unaccompanied children arrived in 2015.

cases.title: Marcial Maciel and the Legion of Christ — 2019 internal report
cases.who: Legion of Christ (Legionaries); founder Marcial Maciel
cases.what: For decades until 2006 the Vatican dismissed accusations by seminarians that founder Marcial Maciel had abused them. In 2006 it ordered him to retire to a life of 'prayer and penitence', and on 1 May 2010, after an apostolic visitation, it said his acts were 'true crimes'. The Legion's own report, released on 21 December 2019, found that 175 minors were abused by 33 of its priests between 1941 and 2019; at least 60 of them by Maciel. It said 111 of the 175 were victims of Maciel or of his victims, and that 14 of the 33 abusive priests had themselves been abused within the order.
cases.cover_up: Letters to the Vatican in 1976, 1978 and 1989 and formal charges in 1998 produced no action; Vatican in 2010 said the Legion had shielded Maciel; Maciel never laicised or tried

cases.title: Romania — post-1989 adoption trade and 2004 ban
cases.who: Private adoption agencies and intermediaries; Romanian authorities
cases.what: After Ceaușescu's fall, television images of about 100,000 children in orphanages led to an adoption boom; private agencies charged €7,500–25,000 and the system 'quickly became awash in corruption' (DW). Romania halted adoptions in June 1991 and, under EU pressure, passed a law in June 2004 banning all foreign adoptions except by grandparents. The European Parliament's rapporteur Baroness Emma Nicholson had criticised 'international adoption and child trafficking' in Romania. Romania's own HCCH return shows 458 intercountry adoptions in 2002, 332 in 2003, 2 in 2005 and 0 in 2006.

cases.title: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)
cases.who: Orphanages and foreign adoption agencies operating in Ethiopia
cases.what: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

cases.title: Italian Bishops' Conference (CEI) — national safeguarding reports (2022–2025)
cases.who: Conferenza Episcopale Italiana — diocesan listening centres and the national child-protection service
cases.what: The Italian Bishops' Conference published its first national report in November 2022, prepared with experts of the Università Cattolica: 80 diocesan listening centres had received 86 contacts in 2020–2021 concerning 89 people, against 68 alleged abusers, 44% of them clerics. CEI also said dioceses had sent 613 files on clerics to the Vatican's doctrine office since 2000. Its third survey, presented in May 2025, counted 115 alleged victims (64 boys, 51 girls) and 67 alleged perpetrators, 44 of them clergy, in 2023–2024. Critics said the reports are too narrow and Italy has no independent national inquiry.
cases.cover_up: Critics, including Rete l'Abuso, said the reports cover only recent diocesan-desk data and omit court and Vatican cases; the first report mentions no reports to civil authorities.

cases.title: Operation Rescue — Boylover forum network
cases.who: Boylover forum (Netherlands-hosted)
cases.what: A forum presenting itself as 'discussion-only' where members made contact before moving to private channels to share abuse images. UK CEOP traced the owner and the server to the Netherlands in 2009; Europol rebuilt the forum offline and sent 4,202 intelligence reports to 25 EU states and 8 other countries. By March 2011, 670 suspects had been identified, 184 arrested and 230 children safeguarded, which Europol called the highest number for such an investigation.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

flows.title: Seoul → Italy
flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to Italy; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.title: Bucharest → Italy
flows.what: Romanian intercountry adoptions to Italy in 2002, during the moratorium period before the 2004 ban.

flows.title: Edo State → Libya → Italy (sex trafficking of women and girls)
flows.what: Women and girls, most from Edo State, are moved overland through Niger and Libya and by boat to Italy, bound by debt and oaths. IOM recorded an almost 600 per cent rise in potential victims arriving by sea in 2014–2017.

flows.title: Italy / Germany / Switzerland → Kenya coast (tourist offenders)
flows.what: The 2006 UNICEF–Government study found Italian, German and Swiss tourists made up 44 per cent of clients of exploited children on the coast; Kenyans were 38 per cent.

flows.title: Phoenix → Rome: Joseph Henn (fugitive 2003–2019)
flows.what: Indicted in Arizona in 2003, the Salvatorian priest went to Italy and evaded a confirmed extradition until his arrest in Rome in May 2019.

flows.title: Verona → Mendoza: Fr Nicola Corradi
flows.what: Corradi, accused at the Provolo deaf school in Verona in 2009 and flagged by the diocese in 2011, worked at the order's school in Argentina, where he was arrested in 2016 and in 2019 sentenced to 42 years for abusing deaf children.

networks.name: Boylover forum
networks.what: 'Discussion-only' forum used to make contact before sharing abuse material privately; 670 suspects, 184 arrests, 230 children safeguarded (Operation Rescue, 2011).

networks.name: Kidflix
networks.what: Paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users (2022–2025), 91,000 videos; 1,393 suspects identified, 79 arrested.

networks.name: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
networks.what: Not one organisation: thousands of local traffickers, often parents or relatives, paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse. IJM: 1 in 100 Filipino children affected in 2022.

networks.name: Black Axe (Neo-Black Movement of Africa confraternity)
networks.what: Nigerian confraternity whose members in Italy were arrested in 2016 for 'mafia conspiracy, drug trafficking, exploitation of prostitution and violent crimes'. A Palermo court convicted 14 in 2018; in 2019 another Palermo court rejected the mafia-association charge for five others.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

networks.name: Legion of Christ (Legionaries of Christ)
networks.what: Founded in Mexico in 1941 by Marcial Maciel. The Vatican said in 2010 that Maciel committed 'true crimes' and the Legion had shielded him, and placed it under a papal delegate. The Legion's December 2019 report acknowledged 175 minors abused 1941–2019, 60 by Maciel and the rest by 33 priests.

networks.name: Congregation of Christian Brothers
networks.what: Irish-founded teaching order. The Ryan Report found sexual abuse 'endemic' in its Irish industrial schools; 11 Brothers were convicted over Mount Cashel in Canada; Australia's Royal Commission found 22% of Brothers were alleged perpetrators since 1950. Its North American province filed for bankruptcy in 2011 and paid US$16.5 million to 400 victims.

networks.name: Marist Brothers
networks.what: Teaching order founded in France. Listed 154 members accused in Australia (1980–2015); nine Brothers convicted in New Zealand; apologised for systemic abuse at Scottish schools; acknowledged at least 14 victims of one Brother in Chile; complaints against 12 teachers at Barcelona schools.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2007: Liberia — post-war orphanage boom and adoption fraud
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found West and Central Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Special Court for Sierra Leone — Charles Taylor convicted of aiding sexual slavery and use of child soldiers (2012)
cases.who: Charles Taylor, former President of Liberia; Revolutionary United Front (RUF) and allied rebel forces he aided
cases.what: On 26 April 2012 the Special Court for Sierra Leone, sitting in The Hague, convicted former Liberian president Charles Taylor on all 11 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity, on the basis of aiding and abetting crimes by the Revolutionary United Front during Sierra Leone's civil war, including sexual slavery and the recruitment and use of children under 15 as fighters. He was sentenced to 50 years in prison in May 2012.

cases.title: UN — Secretary-General's annual SEA reports: 27 child victims in peacekeeping and political missions in 2024
cases.who: UN peacekeepers, civilian staff, agency staff and implementing partners
cases.what: The Secretary-General reports each year to the General Assembly on special measures for protection from sexual exploitation and abuse. The report released in March 2025 recorded 102 allegations in peacekeeping and political missions in 2024, 44 in DR Congo and 40 in the Central African Republic, with 125 victims, 27 of them children; there were also 190 allegations against staff of UN agencies, funds and programmes and 382 against staff of implementing partners. The supplementary tables list child victims in MINUSCA (Central African Republic, 13), MONUSCO (DR Congo, 9), UNMISS (South Sudan, 2), UNMIL (Liberia, 2) and UNITAD (Iraq, 1). It noted about 750 paternity claims involving peacekeepers since 2006, more than 500 still pending.
cases.cover_up: About 750 paternity and child support claims against peacekeeping personnel since 2006, more than 500 still pending; claims are referred to troop-contributing countries, most of which have not taken meaningful action

cases.title: Liberia — post-war orphanage boom and adoption fraud
cases.who: Private orphanages and adoption facilitators
cases.what: After the civil war ended in 2003 the number of private orphanages rose from 40 to 120. In 2005 the Hannah B. Williams Orphanage in Monrovia was closed and 89 of its 102 'orphans' returned to their families. A 2007 UNICEF/Holt International report found many children entered the adoption pipeline through fraud, including false promises to birth parents, and the UN Mission found unaccredited for-profit orphanages. Canada placed a moratorium on Liberian adoptions.

cases.title: West Africa 'sex for aid' — UNHCR/Save the Children report and OIOS investigation
cases.who: Aid workers (UN agencies, national and international NGOs), peacekeepers and community leaders
cases.what: A joint UNHCR and Save the Children UK mission reported in early 2002 that refugee children in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were being sexually exploited by employees of NGOs, UNHCR and other UN bodies, and by peacekeepers, often in exchange for food and aid. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services then fully investigated 43 cases and substantiated 10, including the rape of a 14-year-old refugee girl in a Guinean camp and a UN Volunteer's sexual relationship with a girl of about 15 in Guéckédou; one substantiated case involved a peacekeeper, who was repatriated. OIOS (October 2002) found no allegation against a UN staff member substantiated and said it found no evidence of 'widespread' abuse; Save the Children UK replied that nothing the UN found made it think it was wrong.

cases.title: UN — Zeid report: 45% of 2004 peacekeeping SEA allegations involved sex with under-18s (2005)
cases.who: UN peacekeeping military and civilian personnel
cases.what: On 24 March 2005 the Secretary-General transmitted the report of his adviser Prince Zeid Ra'ad Zeid Al-Hussein on sexual exploitation and abuse in UN peacekeeping. Of 105 allegations recorded across missions in 2004, about 45% involved sex with persons under 18; in MONUC (DR Congo) 72 allegations were received between May and September 2004, and women interviewed described 'rape disguised as prostitution', with sex often costing about $1 to $3. OIOS considered 7 of the MONUC cases it examined fully substantiated and found convincing evidence in 2 more. The report recommended binding standards for all personnel, a professional investigative capacity, on-site courts martial and DNA paternity testing.

flows.title: Monrovia → United States
flows.what: US immigrant visas issued to children adopted from Monrovia, FY1994–FY2014 (peak 353 in FY2006).

networks.name: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
networks.what: UN Secretary-General reports record 357 SEA allegations against peacekeeping personnel in 2006, falling to 51 in 2014 and rising to 102 in 2024. In 2024, 27 of 125 identified victims were children. Most allegations since 2018 come from MONUSCO (DRC) and MINUSCA (CAR). Criminal accountability rests with troop-contributing countries; the UN can only repatriate.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2009: Malaysia — Women, Family and Community Development Ministry task force on the sexual abuse of Penan girls by timber workers (2009).
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 17,046 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (5% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Malaysia — government task force confirms rape of Penan schoolgirls by timber workers in Sarawak (2009).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 282 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Malaysia — government task force confirms rape of Penan schoolgirls by timber workers in Sarawak (2009)
cases.who: Workers of Malaysian logging companies in Sarawak (no company named)
cases.what: A team from Malaysia's Ministry of Women, Family and Community Development investigated in Sarawak in November 2008, and its report, made public in September 2009 after the Associated Press obtained it, found that timber workers had raped or tried to sexually abuse Penan schoolgirls, some as young as 10, including girls given lifts to school in logging trucks. The team interviewed four women with direct experience and many others who said abuse was common; it named no company. Sarawak police said three complaints had been investigated the previous year without enough evidence to prosecute.
cases.cover_up: Sarawak police said three complaints the year before had been probed and none taken to court

cases.title: Global Ikhwan (GISB) children's homes — Operation Global
cases.who: Global Ikhwan Services and Business Holdings (GISB), linked to the banned Al-Arqam movement
cases.what: On 11 September 2024 Malaysian police raided 20 charity homes linked to GISB Holdings in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan, rescued 402 children aged 1 to 17 and arrested 171 adults, after six months of intelligence work; police said they had received 41 reports about the group since 2011. By 10 October police put the total rescued at 625. Three madrasah student assistants in Kuala Pilah were charged with 14 counts of sexually abusing five children in 2022–2023, another teaching assistant with sexually assaulting four boys, and others with physical abuse of children; police said the investigation pointed to organised crime and human trafficking.

cases.title: Malaysia — online baby-selling trade (Al Jazeera 101 East)
cases.who: Online brokers; baby sellers
cases.what: An undercover Al Jazeera 101 East investigation (24 November 2016) documented an online trade in which babies were advertised with photos and sold for thousands of dollars, with buyers choosing by gender, race and skin colour. Some babies went to couples wanting a child; others, it reported, were sold to traffickers. Immigrant sex workers who cannot legally bear children in Malaysia were among those giving up babies.

flows.title: Abuse material hosted in Malaysia (IWF 2025)
flows.what: 5% of IWF-actioned URLs in both 2024 and 2025.

networks.what: Company linked to the banned Al-Arqam movement that ran children's homes; 2024 police raids rescued 402 children and led to 415 arrests.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: New Zealand → Australia: Brother Bernard McGrath; New Zealand → Papua New Guinea: priests sent after allegations; Australia / New Zealand → Fiji: transferred clergy.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: State schools and programmes where removed children were sexually abused
patterns.role_note: British child migration programmes — IICSA (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 2005: New Zealand Crimes Amendment Act 2005 criminalises sexual conduct with children abroad by citizens and residents
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Lake Alice Hospital Child and Adolescent Unit — torture finding; Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care — 'Whanaketia' final report.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 282 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Dilworth School — Anglican boarding school, Auckland
cases.who: Dilworth Trust (Anglican-linked school for boys from disadvantaged families)
cases.what: Police arrested and charged six men on 14 September 2020 over offences at Dilworth alleged to date from the 1970s to the early 2000s. An independent inquiry led by Dame Silvia Cartwright and Frances Joychild KC, released on 18 September 2023 and covering 1950 to the present, found that sexual abuse was committed consistently from the mid-1950s to the end of 2005: 126 of 171 former students who gave information reported being sexually abused, and the inquiry knew of 49 more. Police estimated 233 student victims. The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care also examined Dilworth.
cases.cover_up: The independent inquiry concluded that ongoing silence about the abuse was 'the primary reason for the damage' to former students.

cases.title: Operation Blackwrist — Thai boys abused for Tor sites
cases.who: Tor site administrators in Thailand and Australia
cases.what: INTERPOL launched Operation Blackwrist in 2017 after finding, during routine dark web monitoring, material showing the abuse of 11 boys under 13, published weekly on a subscription website with nearly 63,000 users. Bulgaria's cybercrime police, supported by Europol, took down the servers; US HSI, New Zealand's Department of Internal Affairs, NCMEC and Australian police assisted. The main administrator in Thailand and a second administrator in Adelaide, Australia, were arrested in January 2018. In June 2018 a Thai court sentenced the Thai administrator to 146 years, and an associate received 36 years; on 17 May 2019 the Australian administrator was sentenced to 40 years and three months, the longest sentence ever imposed in Australia for child sex offences. INTERPOL said 50 children had been removed from harm and 9 offenders arrested in Thailand, Australia and the United States.

cases.title: Matthew Falder — dark web 'hurtcore' blackmailer
cases.who: Individual offender posting on hurtcore dark web sites
cases.what: A Cambridge-educated Birmingham university researcher posed online as a depressed female artist to lure victims, some as young as 14, into sending images, then blackmailed them into sending increasingly degrading material, which he shared on dark web 'hurtcore' sites. The NCA estimated more than 50 victims between 2009 and 2017. A taskforce of the NCA, GCHQ, US Homeland Security Investigations, the Australian Federal Police and Europol, with police in Israel and Slovenia, identified him after four years; he was arrested in June 2017. He admitted 137 of 188 charges and was jailed for 32 years in February 2018, thought to be the first UK prosecution related to hurtcore material; in October 2018 the Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to 25 years.
cases.cover_up: The NCA said technology companies' limited cooperation may have delayed identifying victims.

cases.title: 764 network — founder sentenced to 80 years
cases.who: 764 (online network on Discord/Telegram; founder Bradley Cadenhead)
cases.what: 764, named after the first digits of the ZIP code of Stephenville, Texas, extorted minors into producing abuse material, self-harm and animal cruelty. Its founder, Bradley Cadenhead, was arrested in August 2021 aged 16 and on 16 May 2023 was sentenced in Texas to 80 years after pleading guilty to nine counts of possession/promotion of child sexual abuse material. The US DOJ describes 764 as a nihilistic violent extremist network and its Counterterrorism Section prosecutes it; on 29 April 2025 DOJ announced the arrests of two alleged leaders of the subgroup '764 Inferno', in North Carolina and in Greece. On 10 December 2025 Canada became the first country to list 764 as a terrorist entity.

cases.title: Marist Brothers and priests — New Zealand convictions
cases.who: Marist Brothers; Society of Mary
cases.what: A 2018 Otago Daily Times report listed nine Marist Brothers convicted of crimes against boys in New Zealand, including two at Hato Paora College. Marist priest Alan Woodcock was extradited from England and convicted in 2004 of 21 offences (1978–1987). Brother Kevin Healy was convicted in 2020. The church admitted in 2022 that 14% of its diocesan clergy had been accused since 1950.

cases.title: Fiji — transferred clergy and Julian Fox
cases.who: Salesians; Catholic Church in Fiji
cases.what: Salesian priest Julian Fox was moved to Fiji in 1999 after Australian police began investigating abuse allegations; he was jailed in Australia in 2015. The Catholic Church in Fiji knew of the allegations nine years before he was charged. In July 2020 1News reported that some of about 1,300 alleged child abuse cases involving clergy in Fiji concerned clergy from Australia and New Zealand.
cases.cover_up: Fox was transferred to Fiji in 1999 after Australian police began investigating; the Fiji church knew of allegations nine years before he was charged

cases.title: Gloriavale Christian Community — convictions and Employment Court findings
cases.who: Gloriavale Christian Community
cases.what: Founder Neville Cooper ('Hopeful Christian') was sentenced in December 1995 to five years in prison on three charges of indecent assault against a young woman, after an earlier conviction on 10 counts involving five young complainants was overturned on appeal. In May 2022 the Employment Court ruled that three former members had been employees from age six, doing 'strenuous, difficult and sometimes dangerous' work. Leader Howard Temple pleaded guilty in 2025 to indecently assaulting six girls and young women between 2002 and 2022, resigned as leader, and on 12 December 2025 was jailed for 26 months.
cases.cover_up: In January 2025 Gloriavale's leadership said past leaders had not reported known abuse to authorities; in 2026 the Charities Registration Board cited the school's failure to report child sexual offending.

cases.title: Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care — 'Whanaketia' final report
cases.who: State social welfare, disability, mental health, education, law-enforcement and faith-based care settings
cases.what: The final report, made public on 24 July 2024, found abuse was rife in state and faith-based care and that sexual abuse was commonplace, with abusers grooming people in care. It estimated 200,000 of about 655,000 people in care between 1950 and 2019 were abused; Māori were more likely to be abused. Commissioners Coral Shaw, Andrew Erueti and Paul Gibson made 138 recommendations, including a specialist investigation unit and an independent Care Safe Agency, and called it 'a national disgrace'.
cases.cover_up: Commissioners found the state failed to respond to signs of systemic abuse and neglect, and that by 2024 there had been very little progress on the redress system they recommended in 2021.

cases.title: British child migration programmes — IICSA
cases.who: UK government; Fairbridge Society, Barnardo's, Sisters of Nazareth, Catholic Church agencies and others; receiving institutions incl. Christian Brothers
cases.what: IICSA's report of 1 March 2018 found that the child migration programmes were 'a deeply flawed government policy' and that successive UK governments failed to ensure protections against abuse. It found a catalogue of evidence that migrated children suffered ill-treatment and abuse including sexual abuse; Barnardo's suspended migration after sexual abuse came to light at its Picton school, and the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to allegations at its schools in Canada and Australia. It recommended an immediate financial redress scheme for surviving child migrants.
cases.cover_up: Successive governments continued the policy despite years of evidence that children were suffering, including sexual abuse. Fairbridge failed to respond properly to a series of sexual abuse allegations at its schools.

cases.title: New Zealand — Confidential Listening and Assistance Service final report, 'Some memories never fade' (2015)
cases.who: New Zealand state care: residential special education, health and welfare institutions
cases.what: The New Zealand Government set up the Confidential Listening and Assistance Service, chaired by Judge Carolyn Henwood, in 2008 to hear people who had been abused or neglected in state care before 1992. It heard 1,103 participants and finished in June 2015; its final report, 'Some memories never fade', was released under the Official Information Act in August 2015. The panel described 'an alarming amount of abuse and neglect, with extreme levels of violence', including physical, sexual, emotional and verbal abuse, across the 50 years before 1992, and said much of it was preventable with better oversight.

cases.title: Royal Commission into Abuse in Care — Catholic institutions
cases.who: Catholic Church in Aotearoa New Zealand; St John of God Brothers at Marylands School
cases.what: The Royal Commission's final report, Whanaketia, published 24 July 2024, found about 200,000 people were abused in state and faith-based care from 1950 to 2019. It found Catholic responses inadequate, noting a 2020 church briefing that 14% of clergy were accused over 1950–1999, and singled out Marylands School in Christchurch for some of the highest levels of sexual abuse. It found abusers were transferred to other ministries and recommended an inquiry into priests sent to Papua New Guinea.
cases.cover_up: Church relied on psychiatrists' opinions to transfer abusers to other ministries where they reoffended; commission recommended investigating priests transferred to Papua New Guinea

cases.title: Marylands School and Hebron Trust — St John of God Brothers
cases.who: Brothers Hospitallers of St John of God
cases.what: Marylands, a Christchurch residential school for boys with learning disabilities run by the St John of God Brothers, and the order's later Hebron Trust were described by survivors to the Royal Commission as 'hell on earth'. Its August 2023 report found widespread sexual and physical abuse: more than one in five of the 537 boys who attended Marylands reported abuse between 1955 and 1984, and 21 of the 37 Brothers who served at Marylands and in Christchurch faced abuse allegations. At Hebron Trust youths were abused by Brother Bernard McGrath, who has been convicted of more than 100 offences in New Zealand and Australia.
cases.cover_up: Brother Bernard McGrath was transferred to Australia after 1977 allegations and later put in charge of Hebron Trust; victims sometimes required to sign non-disclosure agreements

cases.title: Frank Houston — Royal Commission Case Study 18 (Assemblies of God / Hillsong)
cases.who: Assemblies of God in Australia (now Australian Christian Churches); Hillsong Church
cases.what: Pastor Frank Houston sexually abused a young boy in the 1970s. The Royal Commission's Case Study 18 findings (November 2015) found that Brian Houston and the national executive did not report the allegations to police when they emerged in 1999, and that Brian Houston had a conflict of interest as both national president and the son of the alleged perpetrator. Frank Houston died in 2004 without being charged.
cases.cover_up: When allegations surfaced in 1999, Brian Houston, then National President of the Assemblies of God and Frank Houston's son, confronted his father, who confessed; Brian Houston and the National Executive did not refer the matter to police.

cases.title: Lake Alice Hospital Child and Adolescent Unit — torture finding
cases.who: Lake Alice state psychiatric hospital, child and adolescent unit; psychiatrist Selwyn Leeks
cases.what: Between 1972 and 1978, 362 children went through the child and adolescent unit at Lake Alice state psychiatric hospital; about half were Māori boys. Survivors described electric shocks without anaesthetic and painful paraldehyde injections used as punishment, and evidence was given of children being raped and sexually abused by staff and adult patients. In 2019 the UN Committee Against Torture found New Zealand had breached the Convention by failing to investigate properly; police opened a new investigation in 2020. Psychiatrist Selwyn Leeks denied abuse and was never criminally charged in New Zealand. The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care found many of the children were tortured, and on 18 Dec 2024 the government announced NZ$150,000 redress per survivor and a new Crown apology explicitly acknowledging torture.
cases.cover_up: The Crown's internal policy refused to recognise the long-term effects of abuse, forcing complaints to the UN Committee Against Torture in 2019.

cases.title: Operation Rescue — Boylover forum network
cases.who: Boylover forum (Netherlands-hosted)
cases.what: A forum presenting itself as 'discussion-only' where members made contact before moving to private channels to share abuse images. UK CEOP traced the owner and the server to the Netherlands in 2009; Europol rebuilt the forum offline and sent 4,202 intelligence reports to 25 EU states and 8 other countries. By March 2011, 670 suspects had been identified, 184 arrested and 230 children safeguarded, which Europol called the highest number for such an investigation.

flows.title: Seoul → New Zealand
flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to New Zealand; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.title: UK → New Zealand child migrants
flows.what: New Zealand's Social Development Minister said in November 2009 that 549 British child migrants arrived between 1948 and 1954 and that most were placed in foster care rather than institutions; IICSA lists New Zealand among the destinations of British child migration.

flows.title: New Zealand → Australia: Brother Bernard McGrath
flows.what: After allegations surfaced in 1977, the St John of God order transferred McGrath to Australia, where he later faced 252 charges; he was also convicted in New Zealand.

flows.title: New Zealand → Papua New Guinea: priests sent after allegations
flows.what: New Zealand's Royal Commission into Abuse in Care (2024) found the church transferred abusers to other ministries and recommended an investigation into Catholic priests sent to Papua New Guinea after abuse allegations. Numbers not stated.

flows.title: Australia / New Zealand → Fiji: transferred clergy
flows.what: 1News reported in July 2020 that some of about 1,300 alleged clergy child abuse cases in Fiji involved clergy from Australia and New Zealand, and a survivor advocate said Fiji was a common destination for transferred clergy.

flows.title: New Zealand → Sydney (Frank Houston)
flows.what: Frank Houston led the Assemblies of God in New Zealand from 1965 to 1977, abusing boys there, then moved to Sydney; Assemblies of God investigations found six further credible allegations in Australia and New Zealand. Origin is a country centroid.

networks.name: British child migration programmes
networks.what: UK government-backed schemes run by Barnardo's, the Fairbridge Society, Catholic agencies and others that sent children to Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Southern Rhodesia; IICSA found sexual abuse and failure to protect.

networks.name: Boylover forum
networks.what: 'Discussion-only' forum used to make contact before sharing abuse material privately; 670 suspects, 184 arrests, 230 children safeguarded (Operation Rescue, 2011).

networks.name: Kidflix
networks.what: Paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users (2022–2025), 91,000 videos; 1,393 suspects identified, 79 arrested.
Online network extorting minors into producing abuse material and self-harm; fragmented into subgroups (CVLT, 676, etc.) within 'The Com'.

networks.name: The Com
networks.what: Transnational network of online groups (incl. 764, CVLT) involved in sextortion, child sexual exploitation, swatting and other crimes; FBI public warning 23 July 2025; Europol Project COMPASS since 2025. Start year approximate.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

networks.name: Marist Brothers
networks.what: Teaching order founded in France. Listed 154 members accused in Australia (1980–2015); nine Brothers convicted in New Zealand; apologised for systemic abuse at Scottish schools; acknowledged at least 14 victims of one Brother in Chile; complaints against 12 teachers at Barcelona schools.

networks.name: Salesians of Don Bosco
networks.what: Order present in more than 130 countries. Documented cases include Boys' Town Sydney, the Don Rua juvenate in the Netherlands, US schools, Julian Fox (moved from Australia to Fiji in 1999), and Vatican sanctions on Salesian Bishop Belo of Timor-Leste.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2004: Sierra Leone Truth and Reconciliation Commission report (2004) — girls abducted for sexual slavery.
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2009: suspension: Sierra Leone suspends adoptions (21 May) 2012: closure: presidential commission shuts down HANCI (April) over the 1998 Makeni adoptions
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.role_note: Sierra Leone — Truth and Reconciliation Commission: RUF and AFRC systematically abducted and raped girls aged 10 to 14 (2004); Special Court for Sierra Leone — Charles Taylor convicted of aiding sexual slavery and use of child soldiers (2012).

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found West and Central Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Special Court for Sierra Leone — RUF leaders convicted of sexual slavery, forced marriage and use of child soldiers (2009)
cases.who: Revolutionary United Front (RUF): Issa Sesay, Morris Kallon, Augustine Gbao
cases.what: On 25 February 2009 the Special Court for Sierra Leone convicted RUF leaders Issa Sesay and Morris Kallon on 16 of 18 counts and Augustine Gbao on 14. All three were convicted of sexual slavery and of forced marriage as a crime against humanity, the first forced-marriage convictions by an international criminal tribunal; Sesay and Kallon were also convicted of using child soldiers, while Gbao was acquitted of that charge. They were sentenced to 52, 40 and 25 years, and on 26 October 2009 the Appeals Chamber upheld the convictions and sentences, overturning only Gbao's conviction for collective punishments.

cases.title: Special Court for Sierra Leone — Charles Taylor convicted of aiding sexual slavery and use of child soldiers (2012)
cases.who: Charles Taylor, former President of Liberia; Revolutionary United Front (RUF) and allied rebel forces he aided
cases.what: On 26 April 2012 the Special Court for Sierra Leone, sitting in The Hague, convicted former Liberian president Charles Taylor on all 11 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity, on the basis of aiding and abetting crimes by the Revolutionary United Front during Sierra Leone's civil war, including sexual slavery and the recruitment and use of children under 15 as fighters. He was sentenced to 50 years in prison in May 2012.

cases.title: Sierra Leone — 29 Makeni children sent to US adopters without parents' consent (HANCI)
cases.who: Help A Needy Child International (HANCI)
cases.what: In 1998 about 29 children at HANCI's centre in Makeni were taken to Freetown for medical checks and never returned; parents later learned they had been adopted by Americans. Sierra Leone suspended adoptions on 21 May 2009. In April 2012 a presidential commission shut HANCI down and concluded the biological families 'cannot be said to have genuinely consented'.

cases.title: West Africa 'sex for aid' — UNHCR/Save the Children report and OIOS investigation
cases.who: Aid workers (UN agencies, national and international NGOs), peacekeepers and community leaders
cases.what: A joint UNHCR and Save the Children UK mission reported in early 2002 that refugee children in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were being sexually exploited by employees of NGOs, UNHCR and other UN bodies, and by peacekeepers, often in exchange for food and aid. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services then fully investigated 43 cases and substantiated 10, including the rape of a 14-year-old refugee girl in a Guinean camp and a UN Volunteer's sexual relationship with a girl of about 15 in Guéckédou; one substantiated case involved a peacekeeper, who was repatriated. OIOS (October 2002) found no allegation against a UN staff member substantiated and said it found no evidence of 'widespread' abuse; Save the Children UK replied that nothing the UN found made it think it was wrong.

cases.title: SOS Children's Villages — Independent Special Commission (ISC) worldwide report (2023)
cases.who: SOS Children's Villages (federation of member associations; International Senate); former senior staff
cases.what: An Independent Special Commission appointed by the International Senate of SOS Children's Villages in 2021, chaired by former Kenyan Chief Justice Willy Mutunga with former Delhi High Court acting chief justice Gita Mittal, issued its summary report on 6 June 2023. Using a 'reasonable grounds to believe' standard, it confirmed serious allegations of child sexual and physical abuse in several member associations in Africa, Asia and Central America, and found cover-ups of past sexual abuse and failures to report to national authorities in more than one association. Countries named in the report include Nepal, Cambodia, India, Kenya, Panama, Sierra Leone and Syria. A confidential 991-page part two went to the organisation's Senate and Executive Board on 2 May 2023; in November 2025 SOS Children's Villages International said it was examining whether parts could be passed to prosecutors.
cases.cover_up: Former senior staff in some member associations knew of abuse and failed to act or concealed reports; serious abuse was not reported to national authorities.

cases.title: Sierra Leone — Truth and Reconciliation Commission: RUF and AFRC systematically abducted and raped girls aged 10 to 14 (2004)
cases.who: Revolutionary United Front (RUF), Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC), Civil Defence Forces (CDF), Sierra Leone Army, West Side Boys
cases.what: The Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Sierra Leone released its final report in October 2004. It found that the RUF and the AFRC 'deliberately embarked on systematic strategies to abduct and rape women and girls between the ages of ten and 14 years', using them as sexual and domestic slaves and 'wives'; in a few cases the children were below ten. It also found that the CDF carried out a deliberate strategy of rape, sexual slavery and other sexual violations against girls, and that girls as young as 12 were forced to pay for aid with sex. Of 189 allegations of sexual slavery of women and girls reported to it, 72.5% were attributed to the RUF and 11.6% to the AFRC.

cases.title: UN — Zeid report: 45% of 2004 peacekeeping SEA allegations involved sex with under-18s (2005)
cases.who: UN peacekeeping military and civilian personnel
cases.what: On 24 March 2005 the Secretary-General transmitted the report of his adviser Prince Zeid Ra'ad Zeid Al-Hussein on sexual exploitation and abuse in UN peacekeeping. Of 105 allegations recorded across missions in 2004, about 45% involved sex with persons under 18; in MONUC (DR Congo) 72 allegations were received between May and September 2004, and women interviewed described 'rape disguised as prostitution', with sex often costing about $1 to $3. OIOS considered 7 of the MONUC cases it examined fully substantiated and found convincing evidence in 2 more. The report recommended binding standards for all personnel, a professional investigative capacity, on-site courts martial and DNA paternity testing.

flows.title: Freetown → United States
flows.what: US immigrant visas issued to children adopted from Freetown, FY1994–FY2014 (peak 56 in FY2003).

flows.title: Makeni → United States
flows.what: Children from the HANCI centre in Makeni adopted by Americans without genuine parental consent (presidential commission, 2012).

networks.name: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
networks.what: UN Secretary-General reports record 357 SEA allegations against peacekeeping personnel in 2006, falling to 51 in 2014 and rising to 102 in 2024. In 2024, 27 of 125 identified victims were children. Most allegations since 2018 come from MONUSCO (DRC) and MINUSCA (CAR). Criminal accountability rests with troop-contributing countries; the UN can only repatriate.

patterns.role_note: Chad — sexual violence against girls by the Chadian National Army (UN verified 2022).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 282 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found West and Central Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Chad — Zoé's Ark tries to fly 103 children to France (convicted 2007)
cases.who: French charity L'Arche de Zoé (founder Éric Breteau)
cases.what: In October 2007 members of the French charity Zoé's Ark were detained in Chad as they tried to fly 103 children to France; the charity said they were orphans from Sudan's Darfur region, but authorities found most were from Chad and not orphans. On 26 December 2007 a Chadian court convicted six French members of attempting to kidnap the children and sentenced them to eight years' forced labour, and ordered each to pay €60,000 to each of the 103 children; a Chadian and a Sudanese defendant got four years and two Chadians were acquitted. The six were transferred to France, and Chad's President Idriss Déby pardoned them at the end of March 2008.

cases.title: Chad — sexual violence against girls by the Chadian National Army (UN verified 2022)
cases.who: Chadian National Army
cases.what: The UN verified rape and other sexual violence against three girls by the Chadian National Army in Lac Province in 2022, and in Sudan attributed 4 of 35 cases of sexual violence against girls aged 12 to 17 to the Chadian National Army. In the Lake Chad basin it verified the abduction of 191 children in Lac Province and Diffa.

cases.title: Central African Republic — Deschamps panel finds 'gross institutional failure' by the UN over child abuse by foreign troops (2015)
cases.who: French Sangaris forces; Chadian and Equatorial Guinean MISCA soldiers; UN officials who handled the allegations
cases.what: The External Independent Review Panel appointed by the Secretary-General and chaired by Marie Deschamps reported on 17 December 2015. It examined accounts by boys aged about 8 to 13 sheltering at the M'Poko camp in Bangui that soldiers, largely from the French Sangaris force, and also Chadian and Equatorial Guinean MISCA troops, had sexually abused them between December 2013 and June 2014, often in exchange for food or money. It called the UN's handling a 'gross institutional failure' and found that three senior UN officials had abused their authority.
cases.cover_up: Report passed 'from inbox to inbox'; panel found abuse of authority by the head of MINUSCA's Human Rights and Justice Section, the SRSG for MINUSCA and the head of OIOS, and that staff became more concerned with whether the allegations had been improperly leaked to French authorities than with acting on them

networks.what: UN Secretary-General reports record 357 SEA allegations against peacekeeping personnel in 2006, falling to 51 in 2014 and rising to 102 in 2024. In 2024, 27 of 125 identified victims were children. Most allegations since 2018 come from MONUSCO (DRC) and MINUSCA (CAR). Criminal accountability rests with troop-contributing countries; the UN can only repatriate.

networks.what: Abducted 276 schoolgirls at Chibok (2014) and 110 at Dapchi (2018); UN verified 991 child abductions and 419 cases of sexual violence through forced marriage in Nigeria in 2024. Active across the Lake Chad basin.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 14,039 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman). 1975: scandal: Operation Babylift (April) — lawsuit alleges many airlifted children were not orphans 1999: suspension: France suspends adoptions from Vietnam (later resumed) 2003: reform pause: Vietnam sharply reduces intercountry adoption while reforming its system (2003–2004) 2008: closure: Vietnam does not renew US adoption agreement (expired September 2008) after US Embassy report of fraud (April 2008) 2009: prosecution: 16 tried in Nam Dinh for selling 266 babies for foreign adoption
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role_note: 2007: Vietnam set up a child sex tourism investigative unit in the Ministry of Public Security (2007), the year an Australian NGO uncovered 80 commercial cases of child exploitation by foreigners in Sa Pa
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.
